title: Primary Myocardial Diseases
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers diseases in which the heart muscle itself is the problem: dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Board questions describe a patient, an echocardiogram, a murmur that changes with a maneuver, an ECG, or a biopsy and ask you to name the disease, its cause, or its mechanism. The key skill is deciding whether the ventricle fails to squeeze (systolic failure) or fails to fill (diastolic failure), and then explaining each finding from that defect. If you can connect wall stress, compliance, and preload to chamber shape, heart sounds, and murmurs, you can reason through most of these questions.
prerequisites: Cardiac cycle, heart sounds, and pressure-volume loops (CV-4)
Preload, afterload, contractility, and the Frank-Starling mechanism
Law of Laplace and ventricular wall stress

connections.how: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a model of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and hypertrophic and restrictive disease are models of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
Fibrosis, disarray, infiltration, and inflammation of the myocardium create the reentry substrate and conduction block behind sudden death in these diseases.
Functional mitral regurgitation in dilated disease and the dynamic outflow murmur of hypertrophic disease use the same maneuver logic as valve murmurs.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis both limit filling and raise venous pressure, so they are classic look-alikes.
Coxsackie B virus, Trypanosoma cruzi, Borrelia burgdorferi, diphtheria toxin, and T-cell autoimmunity are causes of myocarditis.

terms.def: A disease of the heart muscle that causes mechanical or electrical dysfunction and is not explained by coronary disease, hypertension, valve disease, or congenital defects alone.
Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally about 55% to 70%.
Reduced ability of the ventricle to contract, so the ejection fraction falls and end-systolic volume rises.
Impaired relaxation or reduced compliance, so the ventricle needs abnormally high pressure to fill to a normal volume.
The change in ventricular volume per change in filling pressure; a stiff ventricle has low compliance.
Myocyte growth by adding sarcomeres in series, which lengthens cells and enlarges the chamber, typical of volume overload and dilated disease.
Myocyte growth by adding sarcomeres in parallel, which thickens the wall and narrows the cavity, typical of pressure overload.
Haphazard, branching arrangement of hypertrophied myocytes and myofibrils seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Movement of the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum during systole, which obstructs the outflow tract and causes mitral regurgitation.
Extracellular protein deposits folded into beta-pleated sheets that stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Inflammation of the myocardium with injury or necrosis of myocytes that is not caused by ischemia.
Transient left ventricular dysfunction, usually apical ballooning, triggered by a catecholamine surge without obstructive coronary disease.

sections.title: Dilated cardiomyopathy: causes, remodeling, and findings

blocks.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most common cardiomyopathy. Its central defect is loss of contractile force. Whatever the cause, myocytes generate less tension, so stroke volume falls and end-systolic volume rises. The ventricle compensates through the Frank-Starling mechanism and neurohormonal activation, retaining salt and water so that a larger end-diastolic volume restores some stroke volume. Myocytes add sarcomeres in series (eccentric hypertrophy), so the cavity enlarges and the wall stays normal or thin even though total heart weight increases.

Dilation becomes self-perpetuating because of the law of Laplace: wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by wall thickness. A wider, thinner ventricle must develop more wall tension for the same pressure, which raises oxygen demand, injures more myocytes, and drives further dilation. The ejection fraction falls, usually below about 40%.

blocks.title: The remodeling spiral of dilated cardiomyopathy
steps: Myocyte injury or defective sarcomere protein
Contractility and stroke volume fall
Volume retention and series sarcomeres enlarge the cavity
Larger radius and thin wall raise wall stress (Laplace)
Higher oxygen demand injures more myocytes
blocks.caption: Each turn of the loop enlarges the ventricle and lowers the ejection fraction further.

blocks.title: Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy and how they injure myocytes
rows: Usually autosomal dominant; truncating variants of TTN (titin) are the most common; also lamin A/C, dystrophin (X-linked)
Ethanol and acetaldehyde damage mitochondria and contractile proteins; may improve with abstinence
Myocyte loss and fibrosis after viral or immune injury
Dose-dependent; iron-dependent free radical injury and topoisomerase II beta damage in myocytes
Late pregnancy to about 5 months postpartum; oxidative stress activates cathepsin D, which cleaves prolactin to an antiangiogenic 16 kDa fragment
Chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection with inflammation and fibrosis, often an apical aneurysm
Loss of thiamine pyrophosphate, the cofactor for pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, lowers ATP; vasodilation adds high-output failure
Iron catalyzes free radical (Fenton) injury; dilated pattern, sometimes restrictive
blocks.caption: Many causes converge on one phenotype: a weak, dilated ventricle.

blocks.text: The findings follow from a large, weak ventricle. Stretching of the mitral and tricuspid annuli pulls the leaflets apart, so they fail to coapt (functional regurgitation), giving holosystolic murmurs even though the valves are structurally normal. An S3 occurs when blood rushing into an overfilled ventricle in early diastole is abruptly decelerated. Low output and high filling pressures produce fatigue, dyspnea, orthopnea, raised jugular venous pressure, and edema. Chest radiography shows a globular, enlarged heart. Stasis in dilated, poorly contracting chambers favors mural thrombi and emboli, and stretched, fibrotic myocardium supports atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. Histology is nonspecific: hypertrophied myocytes with large nuclei, attenuated fibers, and interstitial fibrosis.

Distinguish idiopathic or familial DCM from ischemic cardiomyopathy, in which prior infarcts and hibernating myocardium produce the same dilated, low-EF ventricle with regional rather than diffuse wall motion loss.

sections.title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: disarray, outflow obstruction, and sudden death

blocks.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common inherited heart disease, affecting about 1 in 500 people. It is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, caused by mutations in sarcomere protein genes, most often beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) and myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3). The mutant sarcomeres are hypercontractile and use energy inefficiently, and the myocardium hypertrophies without any pressure overload. Hypertrophy is usually asymmetric, thickest in the interventricular septum, and the cavity is small. Histology shows myocyte disarray, interstitial and replacement fibrosis, and thickened intramural coronary arteries.

The main hemodynamic defect is diastolic. A thick, fibrotic wall is stiff and relaxes slowly, so filling depends on high pressure and on atrial contraction, which produces an S4 and makes atrial fibrillation poorly tolerated. Systolic function is preserved and the EF is normal or high. Thick muscle with narrowed intramural arteries outgrows its blood supply, causing exertional angina even with normal epicardial coronaries.

blocks.title: Dynamic outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
steps: Septal hypertrophy narrows the left ventricular outflow tract
Systolic flow accelerates through the narrow tract
Drag pulls the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum
Leaflet contact obstructs outflow in mid systole
Malcoapting leaflet leaks: posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation
blocks.caption: Obstruction is dynamic: it grows as the cavity shrinks or contractility rises.

blocks.text: Because systolic anterior motion depends on how close the leaflet sits to the septum, the obstruction varies with ventricular size. Anything that reduces left ventricular volume (less preload, less afterload) or increases contractility brings the leaflet and septum closer and worsens obstruction. Anything that enlarges the ventricle separates them. The murmur is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that does not radiate well to the carotids; the carotid pulse rises briskly, then falls as obstruction develops, and may be bifid.

blocks.title: Maneuvers and the HCM murmur
blocks.caption: Aortic stenosis responds the opposite way to Valsalva and standing, which separates the two murmurs.

blocks.text: HCM is the most commonly identified cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in the United States. Disarray and patchy fibrosis create regions of slow, nonuniform conduction that support reentrant ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, and exertion adds catecholamines, a small cavity, and ischemia. Exertional syncope can come from arrhythmia or from obstruction that worsens as heart rate and contractility rise. The ECG often shows left ventricular hypertrophy voltage and deep, narrow septal Q waves. Distinguish the athlete's heart, whose physiologic hypertrophy is symmetric, has a normal or large cavity, normal diastolic filling, and regresses with rest from training.

blocks.title: Predicting the murmur in a dehydrated patient
blocks.text: A 19-year-old with known HCM collapses at a summer football practice after heavy sweating. Volume loss lowers venous return and preload, so the left ventricle is smaller at the start of systole. A smaller cavity places the anterior mitral leaflet closer to the hypertrophied septum, so systolic anterior motion begins earlier and obstruction is greater. Tachycardia shortens diastole, further reducing filling of a stiff ventricle, and sympathetic drive raises contractility, which narrows the outflow tract more. Stroke volume falls, cerebral perfusion drops, and the murmur becomes louder. The same reasoning predicts that lying him flat and raising his legs would soften the murmur.

blocks.predict: In HCM, would a drug that increases contractility make the outflow murmur louder or softer?
blocks.explain: Louder. Stronger contraction empties the ventricle further and accelerates outflow, which brings the mitral leaflet to the septum earlier and worsens the dynamic obstruction.
blocks.check: The obstruction flow and the maneuver table.

sections.title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: infiltration, fibrosis, and failed filling

blocks.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is the least common of the three. The ventricular wall becomes stiff because something is deposited in it or because the myocardium and endocardium are replaced by fibrous tissue. Compliance falls, so a small increase in volume produces a steep rise in diastolic pressure. Early diastolic filling is rapid, then stops abruptly when the rigid wall reaches its limit, which gives the dip-and-plateau (square root) pattern on a ventricular pressure tracing. Contraction is relatively preserved, so ventricular cavity size and EF are near normal until late disease.

High filling pressures are transmitted backward. Both atria dilate markedly, which predisposes to atrial fibrillation and thrombus. Right-sided congestion often dominates the picture: raised jugular venous pressure that may rise on inspiration (Kussmaul sign), hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema, along with dyspnea from pulmonary congestion. Because stroke volume cannot rise by filling more, cardiac output is fixed and exercise tolerance is poor. Constrictive pericarditis produces a similar picture, but the restriction there comes from the pericardium, not the myocardium (CV-18-F).

blocks.title: Causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy
rows: Extracellular AL light chain or transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid
Low ECG voltage with thick walls; Congo red apple-green birefringence; myeloma in AL; older men in wild-type ATTR
Heart block, ventricular arrhythmia; lung and node disease
Diabetes, skin pigmentation, liver disease; may be dilated instead
Prior chest irradiation; may coexist with constriction
Fibrosis of apex and inflow tracts
Children and young adults in tropical Africa and Asia
Eosinophil-driven endocardial injury, thrombus, then fibrosis
Hypereosinophilic syndrome with marked blood eosinophilia
blocks.caption: Infiltrative causes thicken the wall; endomyocardial causes obliterate the cavity from the inside.

blocks.text: In Loeffler endocarditis, eosinophil granule proteins such as major basic protein damage the endocardium. Mural thrombus forms on the injured surface and then organizes into fibrosis that obliterates the apex, the same end stage seen in tropical endomyocardial fibrosis.

blocks.title: Why amyloid gives low voltage with a thick wall
steps: Amyloid fibrils deposit between myocytes
Echocardiogram shows a thick, often speckled wall
Deposits add mass but no electrically active cells
Myocytes atrophy and are separated by protein
Less depolarizing muscle gives low QRS voltage
blocks.caption: In true hypertrophy (HCM, hypertension), added muscle raises voltage; amyloid does the opposite.

blocks.text: This mismatch, low QRS voltage in the limb leads despite increased wall thickness, is the classic clue to cardiac amyloidosis. Q waves without infarction (pseudoinfarct pattern) and conduction disease also occur. Endomyocardial biopsy shows pink extracellular material that stains with Congo red.

blocks.predict: Two patients have a left ventricular wall of 17 mm on echocardiography. One has tall QRS complexes and the other low voltage. Which has amyloidosis?
blocks.explain: The patient with low voltage. Amyloid thickens the wall with extracellular protein, not myocytes, so electrical mass falls while measured thickness rises. Hypertrophied muscle adds electrical mass and raises voltage.
blocks.check: The amyloid flow and causes table.

sections.title: Comparing dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy

blocks.text: The three cardiomyopathies are separated by asking which half of the cardiac cycle fails. In DCM the ventricle cannot empty: contractility is lost, end-systolic volume rises, and EF falls (systolic dysfunction, heart failure with reduced EF). In HCM and RCM the ventricle cannot fill: contraction is preserved but the wall is stiff, so a normal end-diastolic volume requires high filling pressure (diastolic dysfunction, heart failure with preserved EF). HCM is stiff because of thick, disorganized muscle; RCM is stiff because of infiltration or fibrosis.

blocks.title: The three cardiomyopathies side by side
rows: Normal or small; atria greatly enlarged
Diastolic, plus outflow obstruction in many
S3 from abrupt filling halt; S4 if atria still contract
High LV voltage, septal Q waves
blocks.caption: EDPVR, end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (compliance curve); ESPVR, end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (contractility).

blocks.text: Pressure-volume reasoning ties the table together. Lower contractility in DCM flattens the end-systolic line, so the loop moves to larger volumes and narrows. Lower compliance in HCM and RCM steepens the end-diastolic curve, so every filling volume costs more pressure, and that pressure is what the lungs and systemic veins feel. All three share one consequence: scarred, stretched, or disorganized myocardium supports reentry, so ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death occur in each.

blocks.title: Classifying three echocardiograms
blocks.text: Patient A: LV end-diastolic diameter enlarged, wall 8 mm, EF 25%. Large cavity, thin wall, and low EF mean the ventricle cannot empty: systolic failure, DCM. Patient B: septum 22 mm and posterior wall 11 mm, small cavity, EF 75%, mitral leaflet touching the septum in systole. Asymmetric thickening with preserved EF and systolic anterior motion: HCM with obstruction. Patient C: normal LV cavity, wall 15 mm, EF 55%, both atria very large, low-voltage ECG. Preserved emptying with failed filling, a thick wall without electrical mass, and atrial enlargement point to restrictive disease from amyloid. In each case, first decide whether emptying or filling fails, then use wall thickness and the ECG to name the cause.

Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium with myocyte injury that is not ischemic. In developed countries most cases are viral. Coxsackie B virus, an enterovirus, is the classic cause; adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 are others. Coxsackie B and adenovirus enter myocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor, and enteroviral protease 2A cleaves dystrophin, weakening the myocyte cytoskeleton. Myocytes are injured by the virus and then by the cytotoxic T-cell response that clears it.

blocks.title: Causes of myocarditis and their distinguishing features
rows: Direct lysis plus T-cell injury; lymphocytic infiltrate; often follows a viral illness
Triatomine bug vector in Latin America; amastigotes in myocytes acutely; chronic DCM with conduction block and apical aneurysm years later, plus megaesophagus and megacolon
Weeks to months after the tick bite; AV block of varying degree that usually resolves
Exotoxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, halting protein synthesis; myocyte injury and conduction block
Interstitial infiltrate rich in eosinophils, often with rash and fever
Immune complex and autoantibody injury; may coexist with pericarditis and Libman-Sacks endocarditis
Multinucleated giant cells, widespread necrosis; young to middle-aged adults, linked to autoimmunity and thymoma; often fulminant
blocks.caption: Eosinophils suggest hypersensitivity; giant cells without granulomas suggest giant cell myocarditis; parasites in myocytes suggest Chagas.

blocks.text: The defining histology is an inflammatory infiltrate with myocyte necrosis (the Dallas criteria). In viral myocarditis the infiltrate is mainly lymphocytes, patchy and interstitial, surrounding damaged myocytes. Hypersensitivity myocarditis is instead perivascular and interstitial with many eosinophils, and giant cell myocarditis shows multinucleated giant cells scattered through extensive necrosis without the well-formed granulomas of sarcoidosis. In diphtheria, toxin injures myocytes with relatively little inflammation. Because inflammation is often focal, a biopsy can miss it.

Each manifestation follows from the lesion. Myocyte necrosis releases troponin, so troponin rises without coronary occlusion. Edema and patchy inflammation slow and block conduction and create foci of abnormal automaticity and reentry, giving palpitations, AV block, ventricular arrhythmias, and occasionally sudden death in a young person. Widespread loss of contractile myocytes lowers EF and causes heart failure, sometimes fulminant cardiogenic shock. Chest pain may be ischemic-like or pleuritic when the pericardium is involved (myopericarditis), and the ECG may show diffuse ST elevation. Many patients recover fully, but the sequence below explains progression to dilated cardiomyopathy.

blocks.title: From viral infection to dilated cardiomyopathy
steps: Virus enters myocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor
Viral replication injures myocytes directly
Cytotoxic T cells kill infected myocytes
Exposed cardiac proteins can trigger persistent autoimmunity
Lost myocytes are replaced by fibrosis
Remodeling produces dilated cardiomyopathy
blocks.caption: Viral injury and the immune response both remove myocytes; the scar that replaces them cannot contract.

blocks.text: Stress cardiomyopathy, also called takotsubo cardiomyopathy or broken heart syndrome, is acute, transient left ventricular dysfunction triggered by a surge of catecholamines. About 90% of patients are women, most of them postmenopausal, and the trigger is usually sudden emotional or physical stress such as bereavement, an argument, surgery, or severe illness. The typical pattern is apical ballooning: the apex and mid ventricle are akinetic while the base contracts vigorously, so in systole the ventricle resembles a narrow-necked Japanese octopus pot (takotsubo).

blocks.title: Proposed mechanism of takotsubo cardiomyopathy
steps: Acute stress releases epinephrine and norepinephrine
Very high epinephrine acts on dense apical beta receptors
Beta-2 signaling switches from Gs to Gi; apical contraction falls
cAMP-driven Ca2+ overload and microvascular spasm stun myocytes
Apex balloons while the base hypercontracts
Function recovers over days to weeks
blocks.caption: The mechanism is not fully settled; catecholamine excess is the shared feature of all proposed explanations.

blocks.text: Takotsubo mimics acute myocardial infarction. Patients present with chest pain and dyspnea, the ECG shows ST elevation or deep T wave inversion often with a long QT, and troponin rises, but the rise is small relative to the large area of dysfunction. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive disease that explains the wall motion defect, and the akinetic region extends beyond the territory of any single coronary artery. Biopsy, when done, shows contraction band necrosis, the pattern of catecholamine excess. Complications follow from the acute weakness and its geometry: heart failure and cardiogenic shock, dynamic outflow obstruction from the hypercontracting base, apical thrombus, and ventricular arrhythmias. Because the myocytes are stunned rather than dead, wall motion usually normalizes within weeks.

Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is ventricular dysfunction caused by a persistently fast heart rate, most often atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response, incessant supraventricular tachycardia, or very frequent premature ventricular contractions. A sustained high rate shortens diastole, the period of coronary perfusion and Ca2+ reuptake, while increasing energy demand. The result is myocardial energy depletion, abnormal Ca2+ handling, beta receptor downregulation, and subendocardial ischemia, which lead to dilation and a reduced EF resembling DCM. The defining feature is reversibility: once the rate normalizes, function usually recovers over weeks to months. A low EF that improves after an arrhythmia is controlled therefore points to rate as the cause rather than primary muscle disease.

blocks.predict: A 68-year-old woman has chest pain after her husband's funeral, ST elevation in the anterior leads, a mild troponin rise, apical akinesis, and clean coronary arteries. What should her echocardiogram show in six weeks?
blocks.explain: Near-normal wall motion. Catecholamine-stunned myocytes recover because they were not killed; an infarct of the same size would leave a permanent scar.
blocks.check: The takotsubo flow and the paragraph on its MI mimicry.

integration.text: These diseases connect every Part I discipline. Genetics explains familial DCM (titin) and HCM (sarcomere genes) with autosomal dominant inheritance and variable penetrance, and biochemistry explains thiamine, iron, and doxorubicin injury through energy failure and free radicals. Microbiology and immunology explain myocarditis: coxsackie B uses a receptor shared with adenovirus, Trypanosoma cruzi and Borrelia burgdorferi have distinct vectors and conduction effects, diphtheria toxin halts protein synthesis, and T cells or autoantibodies cause much of the damage. Pathology adds the tissue clues: disarray, amyloid with Congo red, granulomas, eosinophils, giant cells, and contraction bands.

Physiology unifies them. Contractility and compliance define systolic versus diastolic failure, Laplace explains why dilation worsens, and preload dependence explains the HCM murmur. The categories have limits: hemochromatosis and sarcoidosis can look dilated or restrictive, late HCM can thin and dilate (burned-out phase), and ischemic, hypertensive, and valvular disease produce similar ventricles, so the history, ECG voltage, and tissue findings decide the diagnosis.

summary: DCM is systolic failure: four-chamber dilation, thin walls, low EF, S3, and functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation from stretched annuli.
Laplace explains DCM progression: a larger radius and thinner wall raise wall stress, oxygen demand, and further dilation.
DCM causes include TTN variants, alcohol, prior myocarditis, doxorubicin, peripartum injury, Chagas, thiamine deficiency, and hemochromatosis.
HCM is autosomal dominant (MYH7, MYBPC3) with asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, diastolic dysfunction, and normal or high EF.
The HCM outflow murmur worsens when the LV is smaller (Valsalva, standing) and softens when it is larger (squatting, handgrip, leg raise).
Disarray and fibrosis make HCM a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes through ventricular arrhythmia.
RCM is diastolic failure from infiltration or fibrosis: near-normal cavity and EF, huge atria, and right-sided congestion.
Amyloid thickens the wall without adding myocytes, so the ECG shows low voltage despite a thick wall.
Myocarditis is inflammation with myocyte necrosis, classically lymphocytic after coxsackie B; it raises troponin, causes arrhythmia, and can progress to DCM.
Takotsubo is reversible catecholamine-induced apical ballooning in postmenopausal women with clean coronaries; tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy reverses when the rate normalizes.

verify: The proportion of DCM that is familial (about 30% to 50%) and the share due to TTN truncating variants vary between sources.
The DCM ejection fraction threshold (under about 40%) and the normal EF range (about 55% to 70%) differ slightly between references and guidelines.
The peripartum window (last month of pregnancy to about 5 months after delivery) follows older diagnostic criteria; newer definitions use the end of pregnancy or months after delivery.

Mechanisms of doxorubicin cardiotoxicity, peripartum cardiomyopathy (16 kDa prolactin), and takotsubo (beta-2 receptor switching to Gi, microvascular spasm) are leading hypotheses rather than settled facts.

HCM prevalence (about 1 in 500) and its rank as the most common identified cause of sudden death in young athletes in the United States are consensus figures; some series list coronary anomalies or autopsy-negative sudden death at similar frequency.
Heart sounds in restrictive cardiomyopathy are described inconsistently (S3 versus S4); confirm what NABNE expects.
The rate and duration needed to cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy are not uniformly defined.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Dallas criteria, Kussmaul sign, Loeffler endocarditis, and takotsubo, or only descriptive terms.
